title: Alexander the Great's Campaigns
intro: Alexander of Macedon became king after the assassination of his father, Philip II, in 336 BCE. He first secured Greece and the north, then led his army east against the Achaemenid Empire of Darius III. The campaigns took him through Anatolia, Syria, Mesopotamia and Persia to Bactria and the Indus Valley.
ending: His army mutinied at the Hyphasis River and refused to go further east, so Alexander turned back, sending part of his forces by land and a fleet along the Persian Gulf shore, and leading the rest home through the Gedrosian Desert. After his death his generals, the Diadochi, fought each other for about 40 years over the territories he had conquered.

stops.text: Facing a revolt after Philip's death, Alexander rode south with his Macedonian cavalry. Finding the Thessalians blocking the pass, he had his men ride over Mount Ossa and came out behind them, and they surrendered.
stops.quote: When he found the Thessalian army blocking the pass between Mount Olympus and Mount Ossa, he had his men ride over Mount Ossa.

stops.text: After stopping at Thermopylae, Alexander went on to Corinth. There he was given the title Hegemon of the Greek forces against the Persians, and there he heard of a Thracian uprising in the north.
stops.quote: At Corinth, he was given the title 'Hegemon' of the Greek forces against the Persians.

stops.text: To secure his northern borders before crossing to Asia, Alexander advanced into Thrace. At Mount Haemus his army defeated a Thracian garrison holding the heights, then crushed the Triballi who attacked it from behind.
stops.quote: in the spring of 335 BC, he advanced into Thrace to deal with the revolt, which was led by the Illyrians and Triballi. At Mount Haemus, the Macedonian army attacked and defeated a Thracian garrison manning the heights.

stops.text: While Alexander was campaigning in the north, the Thebans and Athenians rebelled again. Thebes chose to resist, and the city was razed to the ground with great bloodshed. Its fall brought Athens to submit.
stops.quote: the city was razed to the ground amid great bloodshed and its territory divided between the other Boeotian cities.

stops.text: Alexander crossed the Hellespont into Asia. It took over one hundred triremes to carry the whole Macedonian army, and the Persians decided to ignore the movement.
stops.quote: In 334 BC, Alexander crossed the Hellespont into Asia. It took over one hundred triremes (triple-banked galleys) to transport the entire Macedonian army, but the Persians decided to ignore the movement.

stops.text: The Persian satraps of Anatolia drew up on the east bank of the Granicus River. Alexander attacked at once, broke the Persian line and won the battle, fought in north-western Asia Minor near the site of Troy.
stops.quote: The Battle of the Granicus River in May 334 BC was fought in Northwestern Asia Minor (modern-day Turkey), near the site of Troy.

stops.text: Orontobates and Memnon of Rhodes entrenched themselves in Halicarnassus. Alexander's army broke through the walls, Memnon set fire to the city and withdrew, and Alexander handed the government of Caria to Ada.
stops.quote: The Siege of Halicarnassus was undertaken in 334 BC.

stops.text: Darius took personal command of his army and cut Alexander's line of supply, so that Alexander had to turn back. The battle was fought near the mouth of the Pinarus River, south of Issus, and Darius fled, leaving his wife and much treasure.
stops.quote: The Battle of Issus took place in southern Anatolia on November 333 BC.

stops.text: The Tyrians refused Alexander and killed his envoys, and he besieged the island city with a causeway and, in the end, a fleet. Those who sheltered in the temple of Heracles were pardoned. About 30,000 people were sold into slavery.
stops.quote: Once his troops forced their way into the city, they easily overtook the garrison, and quickly captured the city. Those citizens that took shelter in the temple of Heracles were pardoned by Alexander.

stops.text: Batis, commander of the fortress of Gaza, refused to surrender. The stronghold fell after three failed assaults, and Alexander was seriously wounded in the shoulder. The men were put to the sword and the women and children sold into slavery.
stops.quote: After three unsuccessful assaults, the stronghold was finally taken by force, but not before Alexander received a serious shoulder wound. When Gaza was taken, the male population was put to the sword and the women and children were sold into slavery.

stops.text: Alexander crossed the Euphrates and the Tigris without opposition and met Darius's much larger army at Gaugamela. The result was a decisive Macedonian victory. Darius fled with a small part of his force.
stops.quote: The Battle of Gaugamela took place in 331 BC in what is now Iraqi Kurdistan, possibly near Dohuk, and resulted in a decisive victory for the Macedonians.

stops.text: After Gaugamela, Alexander advanced to Babylon, one of the Persian capitals, and from there went on to Susa.
stops.quote: After the Battle of Gaugamela in present-day Iraqi Kurdistan, Alexander had advanced to Babylon and Susa.

stops.text: At Susa Alexander found 50,000 talents. He sacrificed at the altars and held a torch race, and sent 3,000 silver talents to Antipater to fund the fight against the Spartans.
stops.quote: There, Alexander found wealth that even he had never imagined possible, 50,000 talents, he sacrificed at the altars and held a torch race, then sent 3,000 silver talents to Menes, to give to Antipater in order to fight the Spartans.

stops.text: Alexander took the route towards Persis and walked into an ambush in the narrow Persian Gates, where the satrap Ariobarzanes made a last stand. The Persians held the pass for a month before Alexander encircled them and broke through.
stops.quote: In the winter of 330 BC, at the Battle of the Persian Gate northeast of today's Yasuj in Iran, the Persian satrap Ariobarzanes led a last stand of the Persian forces.

stops.text: Four months after reaching Persepolis, Alexander allowed his troops to loot the city. A fire broke out and spread through it. It is not clear whether this was a drunken accident or a deliberate act of revenge.
stops.quote: Four months later, Alexander allowed the troops to loot Persepolis. A fire broke out and spread to the rest of the city.

stops.text: Oxyartes of Bactria had sent his wife and daughters, one of them Roxana, to the fortress for safety. Some 300 men climbed the cliff at night and the defenders surrendered. Alexander later married Roxana.
stops.quote: The Siege of the Sogdian Rock, a fortress located north of Bactria in Sogdiana, occurred in 327 BC.

stops.text: Alexander gained control of the former Achaemenid satrapy of Gandhara, including the city of Taxila, whose ruler Omphis had complied with his summons. He then advanced into the Punjab.
stops.quote: After gaining control of the former Achaemenid satrapy of Gandhara, including the city of Taxila, Alexander advanced into Punjab

stops.text: In the Punjab Alexander fought the king Porus and defeated him. It was the most costly battle the Macedonians fought. Impressed by Porus, Alexander let him keep governing his kingdom as a satrap.
stops.quote: Alexander advanced into Punjab, where he engaged in battle against the regional king Porus, whom Alexander defeated in the Battle of the Hydaspes in 326 BC, but was so impressed by the demeanor with which the king carried himself that he allowed Porus to continue governing his own kingdom as a satrap.

stops.text: Exhausted by years of campaigning and afraid of the Nanda army, the Macedonians mutinied at the Hyphasis River and refused to march further east. This river marked the easternmost extent of Alexander's conquests.
stops.quote: his army mutinied at the Hyphasis River, refusing to march further east. This river thus marks the easternmost extent of Alexander's conquests.

stops.text: On the way back, Alexander's army conquered the Malli clans, in the area of present-day Multan.
stops.quote: Along the way his army conquered the Malli clans (in modern-day Multan).

stops.text: Alexander sent much of his army to Carmania with Craterus and a fleet along the Persian Gulf shore under Nearchus. He led the rest back through the Gedrosian Desert. According to Plutarch, he lost three-quarters of his army on the 60-day march.
stops.quote: Alexander now sent much of his army to Carmania (modern southern Iran) with his general Craterus, and commissioned a fleet to explore the Persian Gulf shore under his admiral Nearchus, while he led the rest of his forces back to Persia by the southern route through the Gedrosian Desert (now part of southern Iran and Makran now part of Pakistan). According to Plutarch, during the 60-day march through the desert, Alexander lost three-quarters of his army to the harsh desert conditions along the way.

notes: The article dates campaigns in BC; dates here are BCE. It names no city as the starting point in Macedon, so the route begins at Mount Ossa. It gives no year for Corinth (set to 336 from the section on the background), Gaza, Babylon, Susa, Taxila, Multan or the desert march, so those carry c. or 'after'. Left out: Egypt and Alexandria (the article says he marched into Egypt and set plans in motion to build Alexandria but names no place he visited), Thermopylae, the Danube, Cyropolis and Aornos (passing mentions or no date), Mount Taurus (undated). The article does not say where Alexander died or that he returned to Babylon, so the journey ends in the Gedrosian Desert. It says Darius died after Gaugamela but names no place. Wp titles are best guesses: 'Granicus' is the river, 'Persian Gates' and 'Sogdian Rock' are pass and fortress articles, Hydaspes is given as the Jhelum River (the article names the Jhelum only in another sentence), Hyphasis as the Beas River, Gedrosian Desert as Makran (the article names Makran). Tyre's 30,000 enslaved is the article's own statement, though it also says 'it is said' of the destruction of half the city.
